summary: This document defines two additional policies for the Partially Reliable extension of SCTP. They let a sender limit the number of retransmissions and prioritize user messages, so the protocol uses its resources more efficiently when not every message must arrive.

eli5.summary: Sometimes late news is not worth resending. These rules tell the sender to stop trying after a few tries, or to resend only the important things.

questions: what is the sctp limited retransmission policy
what is the sctp priority policy
how does sctp abandon a message
subtitle: Two more ways for an SCTP sender to give up on a message: after a set number of retransmissions, or to make room for a higher-priority one.

tldr.problem: The Partially Reliable SCTP extension lets a sender abandon a user message, but it defined only one rule for doing so, a timeout. Some applications need other rules.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC adds a Limited Retransmission Policy, which caps retransmissions per DATA chunk, and a Priority Policy, which lets the sender drop lower-priority messages when the send buffer is short of space.
tldr.outcome: Applications such as WebRTC data channels and IPFIX can choose the kind of partial reliability that suits them. The policies are optional, but RFC 3758 must be implemented to use them.

today: RFC 7496 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2015. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it builds on the base extension in RFC 3758.

sections.title: Partial Reliability and Policies
sections.content:
The Partially Reliable SCTP (PR-SCTP) extension in RFC 3758 gives senders a generic way to abandon user messages. The decision is made on the sender side only. The exact condition for abandoning is called a PR-SCTP policy (RFC 3758 calls them PR-SCTP Services).

RFC 3758 defines one policy, Timed Reliability: the sender sets a timeout and the SCTP stack abandons the message when it expires. This document adds two more, the Limited Retransmission Policy and the Priority Policy.

Anyone implementing these policies is REQUIRED to implement RFC 3758. The extra policies themselves are OPTIONAL.
sections.eli5: Some messages go stale, so the sender is allowed to give up on them. There was only one rule for giving up, a timer, and this adds two more rules.

sections.title: The Limited Retransmissions Policy
sections.content:
With this policy the sender sets an upper limit on retransmissions for each DATA chunk of a user message. The sender MUST abandon the message if any of its DATA chunks would be retransmitted more times than the limit. The count includes both fast retransmissions and timer-based ones.

Abandoning does not excuse the sender from the usual retransmission bookkeeping. It MUST still do everything else required for the retransmission event, such as adapting the congestion window and the retransmission timeout. The policy also does not change the handling of the Association.Max.Retrans and Path.Max.Retrans thresholds from RFC 4960.

The sender MAY set the limit to 0. The message is then abandoned when it would first be retransmitted, which gives a service similar to UDP, since UDP does not retransmit either. The RFC names the WebRTC protocol stack as an example of where this policy is used.
sections.eli5: It is like telling a friend 'ask me again at most twice, then forget it'. With zero, you never ask twice.

sections.title: The Priority Policy
sections.content:
With the Priority Policy the sender gives a message a priority. When the send buffer lacks space for a new message, the sender's SCTP stack MAY abandon other messages of the same association, on the same or a different stream, that have a lower priority than the new one. Messages sent reliably count as having a higher priority than every message sent with this policy. Which messages get abandoned is implementation specific.

After lower-priority messages are dropped, high-priority messages can go through without the send call blocking (in blocking mode) or failing (in non-blocking mode).

The RFC's example is the IPFIX protocol stack (RFC 7011). Template records would be sent with full reliability. Flow records for billing, security and other monitoring would use the Priority Policy, with security records given a higher priority than monitoring records.
sections.eli5: When the mailbox is full, the sender may throw out the least important letters to fit an important one. Letters marked 'must arrive' are never thrown out this way.

sections.title: Socket API Settings for the Policies
sections.content:
Section 4 is informational only. It describes how the sockets API of RFC 6458 is extended for the new policies. The policy is chosen with the sctp_prinfo structure, which holds a 16-bit pr_policy and a 32-bit pr_value.

For the Limited Retransmission Policy, pr_policy is SCTP_PR_SCTP_RTX and pr_value is the number of retransmissions. For the Priority Policy, pr_policy is SCTP_PR_SCTP_PRIO and pr_value is the priority. Zero is the highest priority, and larger numbers mean lower priorities.
sections.eli5: The program fills in a small form: which rule to use, and a number. For the priority rule, zero means most important.

sections.title: Status and Support Socket Options
sections.content:
Two read-only socket options report how many messages were abandoned. SCTP_PR_STREAM_STATUS reports per outgoing stream and SCTP_PR_ASSOC_STATUS reports per association. Both are used with getsockopt() and not setsockopt(), and both return an sctp_prstatus structure with two 64-bit counters.

One counter, sprstat_abandoned_unsent, counts messages abandoned before any part was sent. The other, sprstat_abandoned_sent, counts those abandoned after a part was sent. A large message that needs SCTP-level fragmentation counts as sent once at least one fragment has gone out, so each abandoned message lands in exactly one counter. If SCTP_PR_SCTP_ALL is used as the policy, the counters are aggregated over all supported policies. For more detail the RFC recommends subscribing to SCTP_SEND_FAILED_EVENT.

A third option, SCTP_PR_SUPPORTED, works with both getsockopt() and setsockopt(). It enables or disables negotiation of PR-SCTP for future associations, or reports whether PR-SCTP was negotiated on an existing one. A non-zero assoc_value means enabled and 0 means disabled. Whether PR-SCTP is on by default is implementation specific.
sections.eli5: The program can ask 'how many messages did you give up on?' and get two tallies: ones that never left, and ones that were partly sent. It can also switch the whole feature on or off.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document adds no security considerations beyond those in RFC 4960, RFC 3758 and RFC 6458. As RFC 3758 notes, TLS over SCTP (RFC 3436) cannot be used with PR-SCTP, but DTLS over SCTP (RFC 6083) could be, and then the security considerations of RFC 6083 apply.

The RFC also observes that using PR-SCTP does not let an association behave more aggressively than one that does not use it.
sections.eli5: Nothing new to worry about. Giving up on messages does not make the sender any pushier on the network.
